questions.q: Define imagery and metaphor in your own words, giving one example of each from everyday language (not from the text).
questions.a: Imagery: Language that creates sensory experiences (e.g., "The aroma of frying onions filled the kitchen" — olfactory imagery). Metaphor: A direct comparison without 'like' or 'as' (e.g., "Time is a thief" — time is equated to a thief to suggest it steals moments). A wrong answer that only gives visual examples for imagery reveals the misconception that imagery equals only visual description. A wrong answer that uses 'like' or 'as' for metaphor reveals confusion with simile.

questions.q: In the story, Holmes says: "They are my favourite covert for putting up a bird, and I would never have overlooked a cock pheasant as that." Identify the metaphor, name its tenor and vehicle, and explain what Holmes implies about the advertisement.
questions.a: Metaphor: The agony columns are a "covert" (hunting cover) and the advertisement is a "cock pheasant" (game bird). Tenor: the newspaper advertisement columns; Vehicle: a hunting ground and a prized bird. Holmes implies he monitors the columns closely and the advertisement was an obvious, valuable clue he would not miss. A wrong answer that identifies only "bird" without the hunting context misses the extended metaphor and Holmes's predatory stance as a detective.

questions.q: Find two examples of tactile imagery in the description of Nathan Garrideb's room (pp. 43–44) and explain how they contribute to the characterisation of Nathan Garrideb.
questions.a: Examples: "a piece of chamois leather in his right hand with which he was polishing a coin" (tactile: smooth leather, cold metal); "the dull dead skin of a man to whom exercise was unknown" (tactile: lifeless, cold skin). These details emphasise his sedentary, scholarly existence and physical frailty, contrasting with the vigorous criminal who later invades his space. A wrong answer that picks visual details ("round spectacles", "goat's beard") shows inability to distinguish sensory modalities.

questions.q: Compare the metaphor "castle in the air" (used for Nathan Garrideb's dreams) with the metaphor "cold mask" (used for Holmes's face). How do these two metaphors reflect the thematic contrast between illusion and reality in the story?
questions.a: "Castle in the air" represents Nathan's fragile, imaginary wealth and hope — an illusion that collapses. "Cold mask" represents Holmes's outward emotional detachment that hides a "great heart" — a reality deeper than appearance. Together they frame the story's movement from deceptive appearance (the Garrideb inheritance scheme) to hidden truth (Holmes's loyalty, Evans's crime). A wrong answer that treats both as mere decorative phrases misses their structural role in the theme of appearance vs. reality.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the extended metaphor of the "three Garridebs" as a narrative device. Does it serve only as a plot mechanism, or does it deepen the story's commentary on human greed and credulity? Justify with two textual references.
questions.a: The "three Garridebs" metaphor operates on two levels: as a plot mechanism (the ruse to empty the room) and as a thematic symbol of how easily fabricated narratives exploit human desire. The will's condition — "three adult men" — reduces identity to a name, making the characters interchangeable ciphers. Holmes calls it a "rigmarole of lies" and notes the "devilish ingenuity" of the invention. The metaphor thus critiques the credulity that turns a name into a fortune. A wrong answer that only summarises the plot without linking to theme shows surface-level comprehension.

questions.q: Write a 50-word paragraph describing the moment Holmes and Watson crouch behind the cupboard, using at least three different types of imagery (e.g., visual, auditory, tactile) and one original metaphor to convey the tension.
questions.a: Sample: "Dust motes drifted in the slanting twilight (visual) as the floorboards groaned (auditory) under our knees; the cold iron of the revolver bit my palm (tactile). The silence was a drawn bowstring, waiting for the snap of release." A poor answer that uses only visual imagery or a clichéd metaphor ("heart pounded like a drum") indicates limited sensory range and derivative figurative thinking.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagery is the use of vivid and ______ language that appeals to the senses (visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory, gustatory, kinesthetic, organic) to create mental pictures or sensory experiences for the reader.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are ______ a mystery novel late at night: the author writes "the fog clung to the cobblestones like a damp shroud" and you instantly feel the chill, smell the dampness, and see the dim streetlamps.
What is Imagery? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Imagery is the use of vivid and descriptive language that appeals to the senses (visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory, gustatory, kinesthetic, organic) to create mental pictures or sensory experiences for the reader.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Imagery?
questions.a: Students often treat imagery and metaphor as interchangeable "figurative language" and write "the author uses imagery like 'castle in the air'".

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently identify specific instances of imagery and metaphor in the text, classify the type of imagery, explain the metaphor's tenor and vehicle, and articulate the combined effect on tone, characterisation, or theme using textual evidence in a structured analytical paragraph.
